questions.question: Why is diffusion training usually more stable than GAN training?
options: Because it never uses neural networks
Because it trains with a single denoising objective instead of a generator-discriminator minimax game
Because it only works on tiny datasets
Because it samples without noise
questions.explanation: The lesson contrasts DDPMs with GANs by noting that GANs play a minimax game that often diverges. Diffusion instead trains one network with a simple denoising loss, so optimization is much more straightforward and stable.

questions.question: What must a denoising model know in addition to the noisy sample x_t to remove noise correctly?
options: The optimizer state from training
The exact timestep or noise level
The final generated image
A human-written explanation of the image
questions.explanation: A sample with light noise and a sample with heavy noise require different denoising behavior. The lesson emphasizes timestep conditioning, usually with sinusoidal embeddings, so the network knows which noise level it is reversing.

questions.question: What does the closed-form forward process q(x_t | x_0) let you do during DDPM training?
options: Skip sampling Gaussian noise entirely
Compute x_t directly from x_0 and epsilon without simulating every intermediate step
Train without choosing a beta schedule
Decode latents back into pixels
questions.explanation: The doc gives the closed form q(x_t | x_0) = N(sqrt(alpha_bar_t) x_0, (1-alpha_bar_t) I). That means you can pick any timestep t, sample epsilon once, and construct x_t in one shot instead of running the whole Markov chain forward.

questions.question: In the simplified DDPM objective from the lesson, what is the network trained to predict?
options: The clean sample x_0 exactly
The beta schedule for the whole run
The Gaussian noise epsilon that was added to the data
A class label for the sample
questions.explanation: Ho et al.'s simplification turns training into MSE between the sampled noise and the model's prediction epsilon_theta(x_t, t). The lesson highlights that this one-line objective replaces more complicated variational terms while still yielding excellent samples.

questions.question: Why does the lesson describe diffusion as 'score matching in disguise'?
options: Because the model ranks captions by similarity score
Because predicting noise is equivalent to estimating the gradient of the log density
Because training uses a reinforcement learning reward
Because the sampler chooses the highest-scoring class
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that predicting epsilon is equivalent to estimating the score, the gradient of log q(x_t | x_0). The reverse process then uses that density-gradient information to walk noisy samples back toward high-probability data regions.
